newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan orders bank to halt operations.
newsitem.headline: Japan orders bank to halt operations.

text.p: Japanese authorities on Thursday stepped in to close a regional bank, the first time regulators have taken such a strong measure to clean up financial problems left from the boom years of the 1980s.

The Finance Ministry said it had suspended most business of Hanwa Bank Ltd, a second-tier regional bank based in western Japan, because the bank could not recover its bad loans and was unable to operate as a going concern.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, however, told a news conference that the failure ought not to cause anxiety about Japan's financial system overall.

The Finance Ministry said depositors would be protected and that such swift handling of banking failures was vital for the recovery of Japan's financial system -- a view echoed by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita.

"The Bank of Japan believes that prompt measures to deal with insolvent financial institutions without delay will lead to the early rejuvenation of the functions of the Japanese financial system," he told a news conference.
Hanwa, employing about 900 people, operates mostly around the city of Osaka in western Japan.
It was the first time Japanese regulators have stepped in to shut down a bank and only the third bank failure since World War Two.
The two other failures, one last year and one this year, were handled by the creation of new banks to take over the failed institutions' business.
Finance Ministry officials told a news conference that in Hanwa's case, a new bank would be set up, but for the purpose of winding up Hanwa's business.
Established in 1941, Hanwa has book assets of about 658 billion yen ($5.92 billion). It is not one of Japan's "big 20" first-tier national banks.
Like much of Japan's financial system, Hanwa was hard hit by the collapse of property prices from the sky-high levels of the 1980s "bubble" era, in which property and share prices soared.

Problem loans at Hanwa totalled 190 billion yen ($1.71 billion) compared with total capital of 20.3 billion yen ($182 million) at the end of September, when the bank closed its books for the half-year, the Finance Ministry said.
Hanwa said on Thursday that it suffered a parent current loss of 33.72 billion yen ($303 million) in the six months to September 30.
Just two weeks ago, the bank had said it expected to post a loss of just 280 million yen ($2.52 million) in the period.
Current profit is pre-tax, including profits or losses from stock sales and other non-banking business.

Last year, Japan suffered its first bank failure since the war when Hyogo Bank, also based in western Japan, fell victim to bad loans. Another small regional bank went under earlier this year. In addition, 10 credit unions and one credit associations have failed since December 1994, analysts said.
The financial markets took the news calmly.
Tokyo share prices held steady and brokers said general concern about financial woes had already been largely factored into prices. But the share prices of some regional banks fell.

The 225-share Nikkei average was up 22.26 points or 0.11 percent at 21,212.22 just before the midday close. The dollar, which dipped below 111 yen in New York on the Hanwa failure reports, was little affected by the news in Tokyo morning trade. It was steady, supported at around 111.40 yen.

Japanese government bonds opened with substantial gains as traders took the view that the Bank of Japan would keep interest rates at rock-bottom levels to help other ailing financial firms. But prices later eased as attention focused on other issues.
